claim: Single-molecule force spectroscopy (SMFS) uses the cantilever tip of an atomic force microscope (AFM) to apply a force able to unfold a single protein.
source: Single-molecule force spectroscopy (SMFS) uses the cantilever tip of an atomic force microscope (AFM) to apply a force able to unfold a single protein.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about SMFS methodology presented in the abstract.

claim: The obtained force-distance curve encodes the unfolding pathway, and from its analysis it is possible to characterize the folded domains.
source: The obtained force-distance curve encodes the unfolding pathway, and from its analysis it is possible to characterize the folded domains.
evidence: This describes the information content of SMFS data based on established understanding of the technique.

claim: SMFS has been mostly used to study the unfolding of purified proteins, in solution or reconstituted in a lipid bilayer.
source: SMFS has been mostly used to study the unfolding of purified proteins, in solution or reconstituted in a lipid bilayer.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical application of SMFS, implicitly drawing on literature knowledge.

claim: The pipeline was tested with purified/reconstituted proteins and applied to five cell types where the most abundant membrane proteins were classified.
source: The pipeline was tested with purified/reconstituted proteins and applied to five cell types where we classified the unfolding of their most abundant membrane proteins.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: The pipeline was validated by overexpressing four constructs.
source: We validated our pipeline by overexpressing four constructs, and this allowed us to gather structural insights of the identified proteins, revealing variable elements in the loop regions.
evidence: This describes the validation experiments performed in the study.

claim: Cryo-EM and AlphaFold have changed structural biology since the molecular structure of possibly all proteins can be determined with reasonable effort.
source: Cryo-EM and now AlphaFold Jumper et al., 2021 have changed structural biology since the molecular structure of possibly all proteins can be determined with reasonable effort.
evidence: This statement references AlphaFold (Jumper et al., 2021) and discusses the impact of these tools on structural biology.

claim: Cryo-EM and AlphaFold determine only the most probable structure and are not able to identify the various configurations visited by the proteins or their mechanical properties in physiological conditions.
source: However, these tools determine only the most probable structure and – at the moment – are not able to identify the various configurations visited by the proteins or their mechanical properties in physiological conditions.
evidence: This is a limitation statement about current structural biology tools based on their known capabilities.

claim: Much of what we know about the mechanics and the structure at room temperature (RT) of cell membranes and membrane proteins comes from atomic force microscopy (AFM).
source: In fact, much of what we know about the mechanics and the structure at room temperature (RT) of cell membranes and membrane proteins comes from atomic force microscopy (AFM) (Al-Rekabi and Contera, 2018; Casuso et al., 2012; García-Sáez et al., 2007; Zuttion et al., 2018) which can operate in liquid environments with nanometric resolution.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to AFM studies.

claim: AFM can operate in liquid environments with nanometric resolution.
source: In fact, much of what we know about the mechanics and the structure at room temperature (RT) of cell membranes and membrane proteins comes from atomic force microscopy (AFM) (Al-Rekabi and Contera, 2018; Casuso et al., 2012; García-Sáez et al., 2007; Zuttion et al., 2018) which can operate in liquid environments with nanometric resolution.
evidence: This is a technical capability statement about AFM supported by citations.

claim: AFM-based SMFS provides a 1D force-distance (F-D) curve which encodes the unfolding pathway so that from the analysis of the sequence of force peaks it is possible to identify the folded domains and their variability.
source: AFM-based single-molecule force spectroscopy (SMFS) uses the tip of an AFM to apply a stretching force to unfold a single protein. SMFS provides a 1D force-distance (F-D) curve which encodes the unfolding pathway so that from the analysis of the sequence of force peaks it is possible to identify the folded domains and their variability (Engel and Gaub, 2008).
evidence: This describes the information content of SMFS data, supported by citation to Engel and Gaub, 2008.

claim: From the 1D amino acid sequence of a protein it is possible to accurately determine its 3D structure.
source: It has been recently confirmed that from the 1D amino acid sequence of a protein it is possible to accurately determine its 3D structure (Jumper et al., 2021), therefore it is tempting to continue exploring which information can be recovered from totally different 1D spectra – the F-D curves provided by SMFS.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Jumper et al., 2021 (AlphaFold).

claim: SMFS has been mostly used to study the unfolding mechanics of purified proteins, in solution or reconstituted in lipid bilayers.
source: Hitherto SMFS has been mostly used to study the unfolding mechanics of purified proteins, in solution or reconstituted in lipid bilayers.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical application of SMFS.

claim: Unfolding experiments have been performed only in less than 20 different membrane proteins in the last 20 years.
source: Although the information that is possible to obtain at room temperature (RT) is of great interest (e.g. it allows studying mechanical stability [Sumbul et al., 2018a; Thoma et al., 2015] or structural heterogeneity [Hinczewski et al., 2016]), unfolding experiments have been performed only in less than 20 different membrane proteins in the last 20 years, most likely because of the difficulties involved in purification and reconstitution.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the number of membrane proteins studied by SMFS, with citations supporting the types of information obtained.

claim: The folding state of membrane proteins highly depends on the physical and chemical properties of the cell membrane and on their molecular partners.
source: Moreover, studying membrane proteins in their native membrane instead of purifying them would be preferable because their folding state highly depends on the physical and chemical properties of the cell membrane and on their molecular partners that might cooperatively function nearby (e.g. in case of oligomers; Maity et al., 2015; Thoma et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on oligomers.

claim: The unroofing method isolates the apical part of single-cell membranes containing membrane proteins with negligible contamination of cytoplasmic proteins.
source: The first ingredient of our pipeline is an unroofing method (Galvanetto, 2018a) to isolate the apical part of single-cell membranes (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1) containing membrane proteins with negligible contamination of cytoplasmic proteins (Figure 1—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This describes the unroofing method with reference to supplementary figures showing the absence of cytoplasmic contamination.

claim: The unroofing method is reliable with ~80% success rate (n=105) with cell types grown on coverslips.
source: The method is reliable (n=105, ~80% success rate) with cell types grown on coverslips.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the success rate of the method based on experimental data.

claim: With non-adherent cells, like freshly isolated rods, membranes were isolated with a lateral flux of medium.
source: With non-adherent cells, like freshly isolated rods, membranes were isolated with a lateral flux of medium (Clarke et al., 1975) (see Methods).
evidence: This describes an alternative membrane isolation method for non-adherent cells, with citation to Clarke et al., 1975.

claim: During the unroofing process, there is absence of any adsorption of cytoplasmic material like tubulin, actin, mitochondria, or free cytoplasmic proteins from the unroofed membrane patch.
source: During the unroofing process, we verified the absence of any adsorption of cytoplasmic material like tubulin, actin, mitochondria, or free cytoplasmic proteins from the unroofed membrane patch where only the membrane proteins that are hold by the lipids are present (see Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in supplementary figures 3-5.

claim: The isolated membrane patches have a height of 5–8 nm with roughness in the order of 1 nm.
source: We verified with the AFM (Figure 1F) that the isolated membrane patches have a height of 5–8 nm with roughness in the order of 1 nm.
evidence: This is a measurement obtained from AFM imaging.

claim: More than 2 million F-D traces were collected from all the samples (hippocampal neurons, DRG neurons, neuroblastoma, rods, and rod discs).
source: Then, we performed conventional SMFS (Oesterhelt et al., 2000) collecting more than 2 millions of F-D traces from all the samples (hippocampal neurons, DRG neurons, neuroblastoma, rods, and rod discs, see below).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the amount of data collected.

claim: Among the obtained curves, ~95% shows no binding, ~3% shows plateau ascribable to membrane tethers, while the remaining ~2% displays the sawtooth-like shape that characterizes the unfolding of proteins.
source: Among the obtained curves, ~95% shows no binding (Figure 1G), ~3% shows plateau ascribable to membrane tethers (Figure 1H), while the remaining ~2% displays the sawtooth-like shape that characterizes the unfolding of proteins (Oesterhelt et al., 2000; Figure 1I) with each tooth fitting the worm-like chain (WLC) model with a persistence length of ~0.4 nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 6; Li et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the types of F-D curves obtained, with citations supporting the interpretation.

claim: The sawtooth-like patterns fit the worm-like chain (WLC) model with a persistence length of ~0.4 nm.
source: Among the obtained curves, ~95% shows no binding (Figure 1G), ~3% shows plateau ascribable to membrane tethers (Figure 1H), while the remaining ~2% displays the sawtooth-like shape that characterizes the unfolding of proteins (Oesterhelt et al., 2000; Figure 1I) with each tooth fitting the worm-like chain (WLC) model with a persistence length of ~0.4 nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 6; Li et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by data fitting shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6 and citations.

claim: For membrane proteins, the term unfolding refers broadly to the tertiary structure, because the specific timing and dynamics of the pullout of a transmembrane segment and the unfolding of its secondary structure is not resolved yet.
source: We point out that for membrane proteins, the term unfolding refers broadly to the tertiary structure, because the specific timing and dynamics of the pullout of a transmembrane segment and the unfolding of its secondary structure is not resolved yet.
evidence: This is a clarification about the interpretation of 'unfolding' in the context of membrane proteins.

claim: The AFM tip becomes attached to membrane proteins mainly by hydrophobic and hydrophilic interactions.
source: The AFM tips becomes attached to membrane proteins mainly by hydrophobic and hydrophilic interactions (Müller and Engel, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Müller and Engel, 2007.

claim: For purely kinetic reasons it will be more likely the AFM will get attached to the C-terminus or the N-terminus, since those typically exert less resistance to traction than a loop.
source: For purely kinetic reasons it will be more likely the AFM will get attached to the C-terminus or the N-terminus, since those typically exert less resistance to traction than a loop.
evidence: This is a reasoning based on the mechanical properties of protein termini versus loops.

claim: If the tip gets attached to a loop, the trace will be very short, and not detected by the analysis.
source: In other words, if the tip gets attached to a loop, the trace will be very short, and not detected by our analysis.
evidence: This is an inference about what happens when the tip attaches to a loop.

claim: The attachment mechanism is non-specific and agnostic of the specific nature of the protein.
source: This mechanism is non-specific and agnostic of the specific nature of the protein.
evidence: This describes the nature of the AFM tip-protein interaction.

claim: The AFM tip was not functionalized in any manner in order to avoid introducing biases.
source: We decided not to functionalize in any manner the AFM tip in order to avoid to introduce biases.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice made in the study.

claim: Approximately 50,000 traces displaying sawtooth-like patterns were obtained.
source: Among the obtained curves, ~95% shows no binding (Figure 1G), ~3% shows plateau ascribable to membrane tethers (Figure 1H), while the remaining ~2% displays the sawtooth-like shape that characterizes the unfolding of proteins (Oesterhelt et al., 2000; Figure 1I) with each tooth fitting the worm-like chain (WLC) model with a persistence length of ~0.4 nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 6; Li et al., 2002). We point out that for membrane proteins, the term unfolding refers broadly to the tertiary structure, because the specific timing and dynamics of the pullout of a transmembrane segment and the unfolding of its secondary structure is not resolved yet. The AFM tips becomes attached to membrane proteins mainly by hydrophobic and hydrophilic interactions (Müller and Engel, 2007). For purely kinetic reasons it will be more likely the AFM will get attached to the C-terminus or the N-terminus, since those typically exert less resistance to traction than a loop. In other words, if the tip gets attached to a loop, the trace will be very short, and not detected by our analysis. This mechanism is non-specific and agnostic of the specific nature of the protein. We decided not to functionalize in any manner the AFM tip in order to avoid to introduce biases. These ~50,000 traces are dramatically heterogeneous, differing in total length, number of peaks, maximum force, etc.
evidence: This is calculated from 2% of 2 million traces mentioned earlier.

claim: The ~50,000 traces displaying protein unfolding are dramatically heterogeneous, differing in total length, number of peaks, maximum force, etc.
source: These ~50,000 traces are dramatically heterogeneous, differing in total length, number of peaks, maximum force, etc.
evidence: This describes the heterogeneity of the unfolding traces.

claim: Cell membranes contain a large number of different proteins, each hosted in different local environment.
source: This is not surprising, since cell membranes contain a large number of different proteins, each hosted in different local environment.
evidence: This is general knowledge about cell membrane composition.

claim: In SMFS it is assumed that the binding between the cantilever and the protein occurs either at the C- or at the N-terminus, and that the protein is fully unfolded by the tip.
source: In SMFS it is assumed that the binding between the cantilever and the protein occurs either at the C- or at the N-terminus, and that the protein is fully unfolded by the tip.
evidence: This describes a standard assumption in SMFS experiments.

claim: Some traces suggest that other events take place: (i) the simultaneous attachment of two or more proteins to the tip, (ii) the incomplete unfolding of the attached protein, (iii) the binding of the AFM tip to a loop of the protein instead of to a terminus end.
source: However, some traces suggest that also other events take place: (i) the simultaneous attachment of two or more proteins to the tip (Walder et al., 2017), (ii) the incomplete unfolding of the attached protein (Tanuj Sapra et al., 2006), (iii) the binding of the AFM tip to a loop of the protein instead of to a terminus end (Figure 1—figure supplement 7C-F).
evidence: This is supported by citations and supplementary figures.

claim: Attachment of multiple proteins results in F-D curves that will not have a recurrent pattern.
source: (i) Attachment of multiple proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 7D): the resulting F-D curves will not have a recurrent pattern; if two proteins form a complex, the resulting spectrum is the sum of the two individual spectra, which causes deviations of the measured persistence length (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of multiple protein attachment, supported by supplementary figures.

claim: The simultaneous unfolding of multiple proteins is characterized by force changes and varying persistence length.
source: The simultaneous unfolding of multiple proteins is also characterized by force changes and varying persistence length (Figure 1—figure supplement 7D,G and Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: If the tip prematurely detaches from the terminus, the F-D curve has similar but shorter pattern compared to a complete unfolding.
source: (ii) Incomplete unfolding of the protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 7E): if the tip prematurely detaches from the terminus, the F-D curve has similar but shorter pattern compared to a complete unfolding (Figure 1—figure supplement 7C).
evidence: This is an inference about incomplete unfolding, supported by supplementary figures.

claim: The fraction of curves that prematurely detaches has been reported to be ~23% of the fully unfolded protein.
source: The fraction of curves that prematurely detaches has been reported to be ~23% of the fully unfolded protein (Tanuj Sapra et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tanuj Sapra et al., 2006.

claim: Binding of the AFM tip to a loop is equivalent to the attachment of multiple proteins.
source: (iii) Binding of the AFM tip to a loop (Figure 1—figure supplement 7F): this case is equivalent to the attachment of multiple proteins.
evidence: This is an inference about loop binding.

claim: If the attachment of the cantilever tip to a loop occurs with some consistency, a recurrent pattern with deviation of persistence length during intersection and two major levels of unfolding force will be obtained.
source: However, if the attachment of the cantilever tip to a loop occurs with some consistency, we will obtain a recurrent pattern with the features described in case (i) (deviation of persistence length during intersection, two major levels of unfolding force, see Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is an inference about consistent loop binding, supported by supplementary figures.

claim: A large fraction of F-D curves will not represent the proper unfolding of a single protein.
source: Therefore, there is no doubt that a large fraction of F-D curves will not represent the proper unfolding of a single protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the discussion of various non-ideal binding events.

claim: Single particle cryo-EM can produce atomic resolution structures, despite selecting less than 20% of the protein images.
source: But inspired by the successes of single particle cryo electron microscopy (cryo-EM), which can produce atomic resolution structures, despite selecting less than 20% of the protein images (Yi et al., 2019), we attempted a similar approach on SMFS data, under the same hypothesis that 'bad' events are likely to produce non-recurrent patterns of unfolding.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yi et al., 2019.

claim: 'Bad' events in SMFS are likely to produce non-recurrent patterns of unfolding.
source: But inspired by the successes of single particle cryo electron microscopy (cryo-EM), which can produce atomic resolution structures, despite selecting less than 20% of the protein images (Yi et al., 2019), we attempted a similar approach on SMFS data, under the same hypothesis that 'bad' events are likely to produce non-recurrent patterns of unfolding.
evidence: This is a hypothesis underlying the clustering approach.

claim: The key tool to recognize recurrent patterns is an automated clustering method based on density peak clustering.
source: The key tool to recognize recurrent patterns is an automated clustering method developed in our group (Ilieva et al., 2020) based on density peak clustering (Rodriguez and Laio, 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 9, see Methods for a detailed description of the algorithm).
evidence: This describes the clustering method with citations.

claim: The clustering approach detects statistically dense F-D patterns occurring often in the sample (clusters).
source: In short, this approach detects statistically dense F-D patterns occurring often in the sample (clusters).
evidence: This describes what the clustering method does.

claim: The clustering method is based on a previously established 'similarity distance' in the context of SMFS.
source: It is based on a previously established 'similarity distance' (Marsico et al., 2007) in the context of SMFS and, remarkably, it does not require to pre-set neither the shape nor the number of clusters.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marsico et al., 2007.

claim: The clustering method does not require to pre-set neither the shape nor the number of clusters.
source: It is based on a previously established 'similarity distance' (Marsico et al., 2007) in the context of SMFS and, remarkably, it does not require to pre-set neither the shape nor the number of clusters.
evidence: This describes a feature of the clustering method.

claim: Channelrhodopsin (ChR1), Bacteriorhodopsin (bR), and the cyclic adenosine monophosphate gated channel SthK were reconstituted in lipid bilayers and used to test the pipeline.
source: We reconstituted in lipid bilayers (Shen et al., 2013) highly purified Channelrhodopsin (ChR1) (Nagel et al., 2002), Bacteriorhodopsin (bR) (Oesterhelt et al., 2000), and the cyclic adenosine monophosphate gated channel SthK (Marchesi et al., 2018; Figure 2A), and we performed SMFS experiments (see Supplementary file 2 for sample statistics).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup with citations.

claim: bR, ChR1, and SthK were reconstituted in vitro one at a time.
source: bR, ChR1, and SthK were reconstituted in vitro one at a time.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Two main F-D patterns were expected for each reconstituted protein sample: one representing the unfolding from the N-terminus and the other from the C-terminus.
source: Since we did not have control of the protein orientation in the bilayer, we expected two main F-D patterns, and therefore two clusters for each sample: one representing the unfolding of the protein from the N-terminus and the other from the C-terminus.
evidence: This is an expectation based on the lack of control over protein orientation.

claim: The clustering algorithm identified two almost indistinguishable clusters for bR.
source: The clustering algorithm identified two almost indistinguishable clusters for bR (see Methods), and the result is in agreement with the fact that the unfolding of bR from the two termini is almost symmetric as previously reported (Kessler and Gaub, 2006; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a result from the clustering analysis, supported by citation.

claim: The unfolding of bR from the two termini is almost symmetric.
source: The clustering algorithm identified two almost indistinguishable clusters for bR (see Methods), and the result is in agreement with the fact that the unfolding of bR from the two termini is almost symmetric as previously reported (Kessler and Gaub, 2006; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kessler and Gaub, 2006.

claim: In the case of ChR1, three clusters were obtained where the second cluster represents the partial unfolding of ChR1 from the C terminus.
source: In the case of ChR1 we obtained three clusters where the second cluster – cluster C2 – represents the partial unfolding of ChR1 from the C terminus because the peaks of C2 match perfectly the first three peaks of the full unfolding (cluster C1), while cluster C3 perfectly match the unfolding from the N-terminus (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the clustering analysis with interpretation based on peak matching.

claim: SthK generated two clusters, clusters S1 and S2.
source: Sthk generated two clusters, clusters S1 and S2 (Figure 2C), as expected (all the clusters are shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the clustering analysis.

claim: For all three proteins, the value of Lcmax is within 5% equal to the total length of the protein minus the free length of the N-terminus (C-terminus) domain if the cantilever tip attached to the C-terminus (N-terminus).
source: For all the three proteins, we observed that: (i) the value of Lcmax – that is, the estimated length of the segment of a.a. stretched in our SMFS experiments – is within 5% equal to the total length of the protein minus the free length of the N-terminus (C-terminus) domain if the cantilever tip attached to the C-terminus (N-terminus) (see Figure 2B and C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and (ii) the force peaks of the clusters of F-D curves colocalize with the unfolded regions or loops of their structures (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The force peaks of the clusters of F-D curves colocalize with the unfolded regions or loops of the protein structures.
source: For all the three proteins, we observed that: (i) the value of Lcmax – that is, the estimated length of the segment of a.a. stretched in our SMFS experiments – is within 5% equal to the total length of the protein minus the free length of the N-terminus (C-terminus) domain if the cantilever tip attached to the C-terminus (N-terminus) (see Figure 2B and C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and (ii) the force peaks of the clusters of F-D curves colocalize with the unfolded regions or loops of their structures (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: When two proteins were simultaneously reconstituted in lipid bilayers, the same clusters associated with the unfolding patterns observed in the single protein reconstitution were obtained.
source: Next, we simultaneously reconstituted two proteins in lipid bilayers (see Methods) obtaining the same clusters associated with the unfolding patterns observed in the single protein reconstitution (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the co-reconstitution experiments.

claim: When all three proteins were mixed together with different relative abundances (1:1:1 and 1:7:20 for bR, ChR1, and SthK), the number of traces per cluster scaled approximately with the abundance of the mix.
source: We finally mixed all the three proteins together, with different relative abundances: 1:1:1 and 1:7:20 respectively for bR, ChR1, and SthK. We observed that the number of traces per cluster scaled approximately with the abundance of the mix (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a result from the protein mixture experiments.

claim: The histogram of the maximal contour length (Lcmax) of all the F-D curves encodes the protein content of the sample and allows a rapid detection of the presence and of the abundance of a given protein in sub-femtogram samples.
source: The histogram of the maximal contour length (Lcmax) of all the F-D curves (Figure 2E) encodes the protein content of the sample and allows a rapid detection of the presence and of the abundance of a given protein in sub-femtogram samples, also providing a qualitative indication on the concentration of a given protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of the Lcmax histograms.

claim: 301,654 curves were obtained from hippocampal neurons.
source: Next, we applied our pipeline to DRG, hippocampal neurons, neuroblastoma, rod outer segments, and rod discs membranes (Figure 3A–E) and we obtained 301,654 curves from the hippocampal neurons, 413,468 from DRG neurons, 394,118 from neuroblastoma, 386,128 from rods, and 106,528 from rod discs.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the data collected.

claim: 413,468 curves were obtained from DRG neurons.
source: Next, we applied our pipeline to DRG, hippocampal neurons, neuroblastoma, rod outer segments, and rod discs membranes (Figure 3A–E) and we obtained 301,654 curves from the hippocampal neurons, 413,468 from DRG neurons, 394,118 from neuroblastoma, 386,128 from rods, and 106,528 from rod discs.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the data collected.

claim: 394,118 curves were obtained from neuroblastoma.
source: Next, we applied our pipeline to DRG, hippocampal neurons, neuroblastoma, rod outer segments, and rod discs membranes (Figure 3A–E) and we obtained 301,654 curves from the hippocampal neurons, 413,468 from DRG neurons, 394,118 from neuroblastoma, 386,128 from rods, and 106,528 from rod discs.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the data collected.

claim: 386,128 curves were obtained from rods.
source: Next, we applied our pipeline to DRG, hippocampal neurons, neuroblastoma, rod outer segments, and rod discs membranes (Figure 3A–E) and we obtained 301,654 curves from the hippocampal neurons, 413,468 from DRG neurons, 394,118 from neuroblastoma, 386,128 from rods, and 106,528 from rod discs.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the data collected.

claim: 106,528 curves were obtained from rod discs.
source: Next, we applied our pipeline to DRG, hippocampal neurons, neuroblastoma, rod outer segments, and rod discs membranes (Figure 3A–E) and we obtained 301,654 curves from the hippocampal neurons, 413,468 from DRG neurons, 394,118 from neuroblastoma, 386,128 from rods, and 106,528 from rod discs.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the data collected.

claim: The clustering procedure identified 15 statistically dense patterns of unfolding in hippocampal neurons.
source: From these F-D traces we applied our clustering procedure that identified 15, 10, 11, 8, and 5 statistically dense pattern of unfolding present in the dataset (Figure 3F–J, the clusters are named with the sample identifier and a unique number for the cluster, for example, H3 refers to the third cluster from hippocampal cell membranes).
evidence: This is a result from the clustering analysis.

claim: The clustering procedure identified 10 statistically dense patterns of unfolding in DRG neurons.
source: From these F-D traces we applied our clustering procedure that identified 15, 10, 11, 8, and 5 statistically dense pattern of unfolding present in the dataset (Figure 3F–J, the clusters are named with the sample identifier and a unique number for the cluster, for example, H3 refers to the third cluster from hippocampal cell membranes).
evidence: This is a result from the clustering analysis.

claim: The clustering procedure identified 11 statistically dense patterns of unfolding in neuroblastoma.
source: From these F-D traces we applied our clustering procedure that identified 15, 10, 11, 8, and 5 statistically dense pattern of unfolding present in the dataset (Figure 3F–J, the clusters are named with the sample identifier and a unique number for the cluster, for example, H3 refers to the third cluster from hippocampal cell membranes).
evidence: This is a result from the clustering analysis.

claim: The clustering procedure identified 8 statistically dense patterns of unfolding in rods.
source: From these F-D traces we applied our clustering procedure that identified 15, 10, 11, 8, and 5 statistically dense pattern of unfolding present in the dataset (Figure 3F–J, the clusters are named with the sample identifier and a unique number for the cluster, for example, H3 refers to the third cluster from hippocampal cell membranes).
evidence: This is a result from the clustering analysis.

claim: The clustering procedure identified 5 statistically dense patterns of unfolding in rod discs.
source: From these F-D traces we applied our clustering procedure that identified 15, 10, 11, 8, and 5 statistically dense pattern of unfolding present in the dataset (Figure 3F–J, the clusters are named with the sample identifier and a unique number for the cluster, for example, H3 refers to the third cluster from hippocampal cell membranes).
evidence: This is a result from the clustering analysis.

claim: Clean unfolding patterns can be detected even in patches of native membranes.
source: These traces show that clean unfolding patterns can be detected even in patches of native membranes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the clustering results on native membranes.

claim: Clusters DRG12, H5, H8, and R3 show repeated peaks (ΔLc 10–20 nm) of increasing force up to 400 pN.
source: We identified four major classes of clusters: Short curves with increasing forces: clusters DRG12, H5, H8, and R3 show repeated peaks (ΔLc 10–20 nm, distance between consecutive peaks) of increasing force up to 400 pN.
evidence: This is a description of one class of clusters identified.

claim: Clusters R6, H7, and DRG10 display periodic peaks of ~100 pN and with a ΔLc of 30–40 nm whose unfolding patterns are similar to what seen when unfolding LacY.
source: Long and periodic curves: R6, H7, and DRG10 display periodic peaks of ~100 pN and with a ΔLc of 30–40 nm whose unfolding patterns are similar to what seen when unfolding LacY (Serdiuk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of another class of clusters with comparison to LacY unfolding.

claim: The majority of the identified clusters like DRG1, H3, R8, and all clusters from the rod discs have F-D curves with a total length less than 120 nm with constant or descending force peaks.
source: Conventional short curves: the majority of the identified clusters like DRG1, H3, R8, and all clusters from the rod discs have F-D curves with a total length less than 120 nm with constant or descending force peaks.
evidence: This is a description of another class of clusters.

claim: These F-D curves share various features with the opsin family unfolded in purified conditions.
source: These F-D curves share various features with the opsin family unfolded in purified conditions (Engel and Gaub, 2008), for example, a conserved unfolding peak at the beginning (at contour length <20 nm) associated to the initiation of the denaturation of the protein.
evidence: This is a comparison with previously published data on opsin.

claim: Unconventional clusters such as DRG7, DRG8, and R7 were found.
source: We also found unconventional clusters such as DRG7, DRG8, and R7: DRG8 exhibits initial high forces and with variable peaks followed by more periodic low forces, while cluster R7 has a conserved flat plateau at the end of the curve of unknown origin.
evidence: This describes clusters with unusual features.

claim: The cancerous NG108-15 cells have few short and not particularly stable membrane proteins compared to neural cells which have many clusters of proteins under 100 nm that unfold even above 200 pN.
source: The cancerous NG108-15 cells have few short and not particularly stable membrane proteins compared to neural cells which instead have many clusters of proteins under 100 nm that unfold even above 200 pN.
evidence: This is a comparison between cell types based on the clustering results.

claim: NG108-15 cells have a higher fraction of long and stable proteins than neurons.
source: On the contrary, NG108-15 cells have a higher fraction of long and stable proteins than neurons.
evidence: This is a comparison between cell types based on the clustering results.

claim: In native membranes, the expected protein profile obtained from mass spectrometry shows good agreement with the F-D curves profile of just few cells.
source: Furthermore, in native membranes we can directly compare the expected protein profile obtained from mass spectrometry (usually obtained from thousands of cells, see Methods) with the F-D curves profile of just few cells (Figure 3K) which shows a good agreement in particular in the region above 100 nm of protein length.
evidence: This is a comparison between mass spectrometry and SMFS data.

claim: A Bayesian method was developed to provide candidate proteins on the basis of information from mass spectrometry and proteomic databases combined with empirical results from SMFS literature.
source: For this purpose, we developed a Bayesian method providing candidate proteins on the basis of the information present in the data from mass spectrometry (ProteomeXchange) and in other proteomic databases (Uniprot, PDB) – combined with the empirical results obtained from SMFS literature (Bosshart et al., 2012; Cisneros et al., 2005; Ge et al., 2016; Kawamura et al., 2013; Kedrov et al., 2004; Klyszejko et al., 2008; Maity et al., 2015; Möller et al., 2003; Oesterhelt et al., 2000; Sapra et al., 2009; Serdiuk et al., 2016; Thoma et al., 2017; Thoma et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the Bayesian identification method with multiple citations.

claim: The Bayesian identification is based on two steps: first, the crossing of information between the clusters with the results of mass spectrometry analysis; second, a refinement using additional information from PDB and Uniprot databases.
source: The Bayesian identification (Figure 4A) is based on two steps: first, the crossing of information between the clusters with the results of mass spectrometry analysis of the sample under investigation (hippocampal neurons, discs, etc.); second, a refinement of the preliminary candidates using additional information (structural and topological) present in the PDB and Uniprot databases.
evidence: This describes the two-step Bayesian identification process.

claim: The first step of Bayesian identification relies on the comparison of Lcmax of each cluster with the length of proteins identified in the mass spectrometry data.
source: The first step relies on the comparison of Lcmax of each cluster with the length of proteins identified in the mass spectrometry data (Chen et al., 2006; Kwok et al., 2008; Panfoli et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the first step with citations to mass spectrometry studies.

claim: By using the protein abundance included in the mass spectrometry data as the prior, a first list of candidate proteins is obtained as well as their probabilities.
source: By using the protein abundance included in the mass spectrometry data as the prior, a first list of candidate proteins is obtained as well as their probabilities (Figure 4A III).
evidence: This describes how the prior is used in the Bayesian analysis.

claim: The SMFS literature contains 14 examples of unfolded membrane proteins allowing a comparison between the Lcmax of the measured F-D curves and the real length of the same protein completely stretched.
source: The SMFS literature contains 14 examples of unfolded membrane proteins allowing a comparison between the Lcmax of the measured F-D curves and the real length of the same protein completely stretched (Figure 4B).
evidence: This describes the data used to derive the conditional probability.

claim: On average, the value of Lcmax corresponds to 89% of the real length of the protein (R2=0.98).
source: Therefore, we extrapolated the first conditional probability of our Bayesian inference, showing that on average, the value of Lcmax corresponds to 89% of the real length of the protein (R2=0.98).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of SMFS literature data.

claim: When the structure of candidate proteins is known, the probabilities are further refined considering the force of unfolding or the position of the loops.
source: When the structure of candidate proteins is known (helices, sheets), these probabilities are further refined considering for example, the force of unfolding or the position of the loops which are known to constrain the possible unfolding patterns (Figure 4C–F, see Methods for the formal description).
evidence: This describes the refinement step of the Bayesian analysis.

claim: The Bayesian method allows to reduce the number of possible candidates from hundreds to one to four proteins.
source: Like in mass spectrometry, this identification is probabilistic (Figure 5), and it allows to reduce the number of possible candidates from hundreds to one to four proteins.
evidence: This describes the outcome of the Bayesian identification.

claim: Reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction and western blot analysis confirm that TMEM16F, TRPC1, TRPC5, and TRPC6 are abundantly expressed in neuroblastoma NG108-15 cells.
source: To prove the reliability of the proposed pipeline protocol, we focused on four clusters found in NG108-15 cells where the Bayesian method assigned a high probability to the membrane proteins TMEM16F, TRPC1, TRPC5, and TRPC6. Reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction and western blot analysis (Wu et al., 2007; Figure 6—figure supplement 1) confirm that these membrane proteins are abundantly expressed in neuroblastoma NG108-15 cells.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and western blot data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The construct 6xHis-N2B-protein-GFP was overexpressed, where protein is the molecular candidate to be validated.
source: We overexpressed the construct 6xHis-N2B-protein-GFP, where protein is the molecular candidate to be validated (Figure 6A–B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the validation experiment.

claim: The N2B is a chain of 204 aa which can be unfolded with a force less than 10 pN providing a well-known signature.
source: The N2B is a chain of 204 aa which can be unfolded with a force less than 10 pN providing a well-known signature (Linke and Grützner, 2008), and GFP is the green fluorescent protein used to identify which NG108-15 cell was successfully transfected, and if the proteins were present in the unroofed membrane patch (Figure 6C).
evidence: This describes the N2B tag with citation.

claim: The clusters obtained without overexpression (NG8, NG4, NG5, and NG11) were compared with the new clusters obtained from the unfolding of the constructs N2B-TMEM16F-GFP, N2B-TRPC1-GFP, N2B-TRCP5-GFP, and N2B-TRPC6-GFP from the transfected cells.
source: We compared the clusters obtained without overexpression (NG8, NG4, NG5, and NG11) with the new clusters obtained from the unfolding of the constructs N2B-TMEM16F-GFP, N2B-TRPC1-GFP, N2B-TRCP5-GFP, and N2B-TRPC6-GFP from the transfected cells (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This describes the comparison between wild-type and overexpression data.

claim: The F-D traces from transfected cells had the well-known signature of the N2B domain consisting in a flat portion with a length of ~85 nm, which was followed by force peaks almost exactly matching those observed in the corresponding density plots.
source: These F-D traces had the well-known signature of the N2B domain consisting in a flat portion with a length of ~85 nm, which was followed by force peaks almost exactly matching those observed in the corresponding density plots (Figure 6D).
evidence: This describes the validation result showing matching patterns.

claim: The matching was confirmed by the correspondence of the cumulative peaks observed in the global histogram of the contour length of the NG8, NG4, NG5, and NG11 clusters with those obtained from neuroblastoma cells transfected with the constructs translated by ~85 nm because of the presence of the N2B.
source: This matching was also confirmed by the correspondence of the cumulative peaks observed in the global histogram of the contour length of the NG8, NG4, NG5, and NG11 clusters with those obtained from neuroblastoma cells transfected with the constructs N2B-TMEM16F-GFP, N2B-TRPC1-GFP, N2B-TRCP5-GFP, and N2B-TRPC6-GFP translated of ~85 nm because of the presence of the N2B (Figure 6E).
evidence: This describes additional validation through histogram comparison.

claim: The pipeline demonstrates that from the obtained clusters it is possible to derive the unfolding spectra of membrane proteins in their almost-native conditions without the need of purification.
source: This pipeline demonstrates that from the obtained clusters (Figure 3) it is possible to derive the unfolding spectra of membrane proteins in their almost-native conditions without the need of purification.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation experiments.

claim: The superposition of the peaks confirms the identification and allows to map the unfolding positions along the tertiary structure of the proteins.
source: The superposition of the peaks (Figure 6D–E) confirms the identification and allows to map the unfolding positions along the tertiary structure of the proteins (Figure 6F).
evidence: This describes the structural information obtained from the validation.

claim: SMFS detects the unfolded domains of a protein and can characterize their variability where cryo-EM precisely determines the position of the atoms of the well-folded domains.
source: SMFS detects the unfolded domains of a protein and can characterize their variability where the more powerful cryo-EM precisely determines the position of the atoms of the well-folded domains.
evidence: This is a comparison of the capabilities of SMFS and cryo-EM.

claim: The unfolding of the construct N2B-TRPC6-GFP as well as the endogenous TRPC6 show force peaks at 143, 193, and 230 nm with different properties.
source: The unfolding of the construct N2B-TRPC6-GFP as well as the endogenous TRPC6 show force peaks at 143, 193, and 230 nm with different properties (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a result from the TRPC6 unfolding analysis.

claim: The peak at 143 nm is always well defined, but the force peaks at 193 and 230 nm show variability in the location and strength of the secondary peaks.
source: The peak at 143 nm is always well defined, but the force peaks at 193 and 230 nm – occurring at the extracellular loop E1 between S1 and S2 and at the extracellular loop E2 between S3 and S4, respectively (see positions in Figure 7B) – show variability in the location and strength of the secondary peaks (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This describes the variability observed in TRPC6 unfolding.

claim: The unfolding behavior observed at 193 and 230 nm reflects the presence of small structural elements which are present in some but not all instances.
source: The unfolding behavior observed at 193 and 230 nm reflects the presence of small structural elements (Yu et al., 2017) which are present in some but not all instances (see inserts in Figure 7D–E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the variability with citation.

claim: The peak at 143 nm shows a clear and reproducible unfolding behavior typical of a defined and well-folded structure.
source: The peak at 143 nm in contrast shows a clear and reproducible unfolding behavior (Figure 7C) typical of a defined and well-folded structure (Rico et al., 2013; Takahashi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on well-folded structures.

claim: There are three published cryo-EM structures of TRPC6.
source: In the light of these results, we analyzed the available cryo-EM structures of TRPC6. There are three published structures (Bai et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2018); these three cryo-EM structures are very similar – and almost identical – particularly in the long transmembrane α-helices, but differ in the connecting loops where short α-helices are present only in some of these structures (Figure 7C–E, inserts).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The three cryo-EM structures of TRPC6 are very similar and almost identical, particularly in the long transmembrane α-helices, but differ in the connecting loops where short α-helices are present only in some of these structures.
source: In the light of these results, we analyzed the available cryo-EM structures of TRPC6. There are three published structures (Bai et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2018); these three cryo-EM structures are very similar – and almost identical – particularly in the long transmembrane α-helices, but differ in the connecting loops where short α-helices are present only in some of these structures (Figure 7C–E, inserts).
evidence: This is a comparison of the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The short α-helices in the loops E1 and E2 are the small structural elements at the origin of the segmentation observed in the F-D traces.
source: These short α-helices in the loops E1 and E2 are the small structural elements at the origin of the segmentation observed in the F-D traces (Figure 7D–E).
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the cryo-EM structures to the SMFS data.

claim: The most likely conclusion from the SMFS data is that, at RT and in their native environment, the different cryo-EM structures coexist and the connecting loops E1 and E2 have a variable structure.
source: However, as shown in the structures in yellow, the α-helices are not always observed as the single-peak F-D curves suggest. Therefore, the most likely conclusion from our SMFS data is that, at RT and in their native environment, the different cryo-EM structures coexist and the connecting loops E1 and E2 have a variable structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SMFS data and comparison with cryo-EM structures.

claim: The observed variability is not restricted only to loop E1 and E2 of TRPC6: also the loop pre-S1 and S1 of TRPC5 shows a similarly complex unfolding behavior.
source: The observed variability is not restricted only to loop E1 and E2 of TRPC6: also the loop pre-S1 and S1 of TRPC5 shows a similarly complex unfolding behavior as opposed to the unfolding of the loop between S2 and S3.
evidence: This extends the observation of variability to TRPC5.

claim: Clusters DRG5 or H3 show a dual nature: secondary peaks and unfolding humps.
source: Clusters DRG5 or H3 show an even more exotic behavior. Their unfolding curves show a dual nature: secondary peaks and unfolding humps (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes unusual unfolding behavior in certain clusters.

claim: After the clustering procedure, the protein profiles show the presence of structures in the data that have a straightforward correspondence with the samples.
source: But after the clustering procedure described in this manuscript, that requires minimal interventions by the user, we could obtain the black profiles in Figure 2E which clearly show the presence of structures in the data that have a straightforward correspondence with the samples.
evidence: This describes the outcome of the clustering procedure.

claim: The protein profile can be considered as the minimal 2D representation of the SMFS dataset and a 'first-hand information' on the mass/length of the proteins in the sample.
source: This protein profile can be considered as the minimal 2D representation of the SMFS dataset, but more importantly a 'first-hand information' on the mass/length of the proteins in the sample.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the protein profile represents.

claim: The similarity between mass spectrometry and SMFS protein profiles is remarkable considering the several orders of magnitude difference on the amount of sample used by the two techniques.
source: The solid lines show broader peaks and the distributions are not matching perfectly, but we think that the similarity is still remarkable considering the several orders of magnitude difference on the amount of sample used by the two techniques.
evidence: This is a comparison between mass spectrometry and SMFS with consideration of sample amounts.

claim: Protein length detection of SMFS – restricted to clustered traces – provides a semi-quantitative proxy for mass detection at the single-cell membrane level.
source: To become quantitatively reliable, this approach still needs appropriate improvements, but these results suggest that protein length detection of SMFS – restricted to clustered traces – provides a semi-quantitative proxy for mass detection at the single-cell membrane level.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the potential of SMFS for protein profiling.

claim: These results may pave the way to single-cell proteomics and phenotyping, with the potential to advance our understanding of disease development, progress, and treatment effects.
source: These results may pave the way to single-cell proteomics and phenotyping, with the potential to advance our understanding of disease development, progress, and treatment effects.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications.

claim: By combining SMFS on native membrane patches with information present in databases, a probabilistic identification of groups of proteins is possible.
source: Given the high diversity of membrane proteins in cells, the unequivocal identification of unlabeled proteins from single cells is a daunting task. The present manuscript shows that by combining SMFS on native membrane patches with information present in databases, a probabilistic identification of groups of proteins is possible.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: The approach provides usually less than four candidates (p>95%) for most of the identified clusters of F-D traces.
source: Our approach provides usually less than four candidates (Figure 5) for most of the identified clusters of F-D traces (p>95%), and we were able to prove the validity of the identification by properly engineered constructs (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the identification accuracy.

claim: The validity of the identification was proven by properly engineered constructs.
source: Our approach provides usually less than four candidates (Figure 5) for most of the identified clusters of F-D traces (p>95%), and we were able to prove the validity of the identification by properly engineered constructs (Figure 6).
evidence: This refers to the validation experiments with N2B-tagged constructs.

claim: The proposed pipeline offers the possibility to enrich the structural information usually derived from cryo-EM, with insights obtained by unfolding the proteins in their native environment.
source: The proposed pipeline offers the possibility to enrich the structural information usually derived from cryo-EM, with insights obtained by unfolding the proteins in their native environment.
evidence: This is a statement about the complementary nature of SMFS and cryo-EM.

claim: SMFS cannot distinguish between a β-sheet and an α-helix, but it can determine with a good accuracy the unfolded domains of a membrane protein at RT.
source: SMFS cannot distinguish between a β-sheet and an α-helix, but it can determine with a good accuracy the unfolded domains of a membrane protein at RT (see Figure 7; Engel and Gaub, 2008).
evidence: This describes the capabilities and limitations of SMFS with citation.

claim: Cryo-EM cannot capture the structural heterogeneity of the poorly folded regions, while SMFS can provide important complementary information about the mechanical stability of connecting loops.
source: Cryo-EM cannot capture the structural heterogeneity of the poorly folded regions, while SMFS can provide important complementary information, for instance about the mechanical stability of connecting loops.
evidence: This is a comparison of the capabilities of cryo-EM and SMFS.

claim: The pipeline offers the possibility to obtain the unfolding profile of the membrane proteins from a limited amount of native material (membranes isolated from 1 to 10 cells).
source: The pipeline, in addition, offers the possibility to obtain the unfolding profile of the membrane proteins from a limited amount of native material (membranes isolated from 1 to 10 cells).
evidence: This describes an advantage of the method in terms of sample requirements.

claim: The unfolding profile of membrane proteins can be used as a fingerprint to characterize the sample under investigation.
source: We have shown that the unfolding profile of membrane proteins can be used as a fingerprint to characterize the sample under investigation (see Figures 2–3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion about the use of unfolding profiles.

claim: This approach can be extended to characterize, and eventually distinguish, membranes in cells in healthy and sick conditions where other methodology cannot be applied because of sample scarcity.
source: We foresee that this approach can be extended to characterize, and eventually distinguish, membranes in cells in healthy and sick conditions where other methodology cannot be applied because of sample scarcity (e.g. samples from patients).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications.

claim: The unfolding of a protein is stochastic in nature because it can be viewed as Brownian diffusion of a particle in a tilted energy landscape.
source: The unfolding of a protein is stochastic in nature because it can be viewed as Brownian diffusion of a particle in a tilted energy landscape (Engel and Gaub, 2008; Yu et al., 2017), therefore variability in F-D curves is intrinsic to the technique.
evidence: This is supported by citations describing the stochastic nature of protein unfolding.

claim: Variability in F-D curves is intrinsic to the SMFS technique.
source: The unfolding of a protein is stochastic in nature because it can be viewed as Brownian diffusion of a particle in a tilted energy landscape (Engel and Gaub, 2008; Yu et al., 2017), therefore variability in F-D curves is intrinsic to the technique.
evidence: This follows from the stochastic nature of protein unfolding.

claim: The variability in F-D curves is not unconstrained: the energy landscape of a membrane protein has obligatory intermediates that allow to cluster the F-D curves coming from the same protein.
source: But this variability is not unconstrained: the energy landscape of a membrane protein has obligatory intermediates that allow to cluster the F-D curves coming from the same protein (Marsico et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marsico et al., 2007.

claim: The variation of an obligatory intermediate, or a new force peak/a shift of a force peak, is a strong evidence of a conformational change in the system.
source: The variation of an obligatory intermediate, or, in other words, a new force peak/a shift of a force peak, is a strong evidence of a conformational change in the system (Maity et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maity et al., 2015.

claim: Minor unfolding features can provide evidence of mechanical plasticity or structural segmentations of apparently continuous structures.
source: Minor unfolding features can also provide evidence of mechanical plasticity (Takahashi et al., 2018) or structural segmentations of apparently continuous structures (Yu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on mechanical plasticity and structural segmentation.

claim: The result of a pulling experiment of a membrane protein is strictly speaking not a single biomolecule event.
source: Here, we want to stress that we are referring to the 'system' protein plus the surrounding environment and not to the protein only. The result of a pulling experiment of a membrane protein, as opposed to globular proteins, is strictly speaking not a single biomolecule event.
evidence: This is a clarification about the nature of membrane protein unfolding experiments.

claim: A membrane protein does not exist in isolation because at least it needs lipids, but very often it forms oligomers with other proteins or even more complex structures.
source: A membrane protein does not exist in isolation because at least it needs lipids, but very often it forms oligomers with other proteins or even more complex structures like G-protein-coupled receptors.
evidence: This is general knowledge about membrane proteins.

claim: To study the mechanical stability of a membrane protein it is preferable to have it in its physiological environment.
source: Therefore, to study the mechanical stability of a membrane protein it is preferable to have it in its physiological environment, whether it is composed of only lipids or other partner proteins that concur in the stabilization of the structure (like in the CNG tetramer; Maity et al., 2015; Napolitano et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on membrane protein complexes.

claim: A major limitation of the proposed pipeline is the possibility to merge in the same cluster unfolding traces of proteins with a different molecular identity.
source: A major limitation of the proposed pipeline – in its present form – is the possibility to merge in the same cluster unfolding traces of proteins with a different molecular identity: indeed, from the mass spectrometry data it is clear that different proteins can have the same – or approximately the same – molecular weight, a similar unfolding pattern and a similar total unfolded length Lc.
evidence: This is a discussion of a limitation of the method.

claim: This issue is rather significant for short proteins, that is, those with values of Lc between 50 and 150 nm.
source: This issue is rather significant for short proteins, that is, those with values of Lc between 50 and 150 nm.
evidence: This specifies where the limitation is most significant.

claim: In order to overcome this limitation, it will be desirable to couple SMFS with a device able to identify, even qualitatively, specific amino acids during the unfolding process.
source: In order to overcome this limitation, it will be desirable to couple SMFS with a device (e.g. solid-state nanopores; Lee et al., 2018) able to identify, even qualitatively, specific amino acids during the unfolding process.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future improvement with citation.

claim: In the range between 50 and 150 nm, a number of F-D curves resulting from arbitrary attachment or detachment are expected to pass the quality filter.
source: In the range between 50 and 150 nm, we also expect a number of F-D curves resulting from arbitrary attachment or detachment to pass the quality filter (see Methods Block 2).
evidence: This is an expectation about the quality filter.

claim: Given their arbitrariness, the similarity distance will position arbitrary attachment/detachment curves at the edge of dense clusters so they will not be central in the analysis.
source: But in this case, given their arbitrariness, the similarity distance will position them at the edge of dense clusters so they will not be central in the analysis.
evidence: This is a reasoning about how arbitrary events will be handled by the clustering.

claim: It is not trivial to assess a priori the expected maximal contour length (max Lc) simply by knowing the length of the protein measured by mass spectrometry.
source: An underlying technical problem is that it is not trivial to assess a priori the expected maximal contour length (max Lc) simply by knowing the length of the protein measured by mass spectrometry (which usually corresponds to the nominal length: Number of amino acids * 0.4 nm).
evidence: This describes a technical challenge in the analysis.

claim: The difference between the measured max Lc and the nominal length depends on the specific anchoring points of the protein.
source: The difference between the two lengths depends on the specific anchoring points of the protein: the measured max Lc corresponds to the length of the chain between the tip of the AFM and the last amino acid anchored to the membrane during the pulling.
evidence: This explains the source of the difference between measured and nominal lengths.

claim: In experiments on reconstituted proteins and in many reports from the literature, the last anchored point is the last amino acid of the last transmembrane segment (within error).
source: In our experiments on reconstituted proteins (see Figure 2A–D), and in many reports from the literature (Kawamura et al., 2013; Kessler and Gaub, 2006; Möller et al., 2003), the last anchored point is the last amino acid of the last transmembrane segment (within error).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: Applying the heuristic that the last anchored point is the last amino acid of the last transmembrane segment to all proteins in the mass spectrometry dataset is not feasible because the structure of many proteins is not known.
source: However, applying these heuristics to all the proteins present in the mass spectrometry dataset is not feasible because the structure of many of those proteins is not known, and even if known, the error on this estimate is difficult to be assessed.
evidence: This explains why a simple heuristic cannot be applied universally.

claim: A Bayesian framework was used because it is more flexible and naturally provides an error estimate of the results.
source: We decided to use a Bayesian framework that is more flexible and that naturally provides an error estimate of the results.
evidence: This explains the choice of the Bayesian approach.

claim: In the Bayesian framework, the nominal length was rescaled with the probability distribution showing that the max Lc is equal to 89% of the length measured by mass spectroscopy on average.
source: In our framework we rescaled the nominal length with the probability distribution shown in Figure 4C. Based on the 14 references found in the literature, the max Lc is equal to 89% of the length measured by mass spectroscopy on average.
evidence: This describes the rescaling used in the Bayesian framework.

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficient between max Lc and the length measured by mass spectroscopy is r=0.991, reflecting a very good correlation.
source: The Pearson correlation coefficient is r=0.991, reflecting a very good correlation between the two quantities (see Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of the correlation.

claim: The Bayesian approach is scalable and easier to be updated when new data will become available from the literature.
source: Therefore, we think that this approach is more scalable, and easier to be updated when new data will become available from the literature.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the Bayesian approach.

claim: The Bayesian approach is robust in case of a large conformational change of a protein as long as the last anchoring point does not change more than 10% of the max Lc.
source: The Bayesian approach we used is also robust in case of a large conformational change of a protein as long as the last anchoring point does not change more than 10% of the max Lc.
evidence: This describes the robustness of the Bayesian approach.

claim: The max Lc has the higher weight in the probability estimation while the contribution of the correlation of the peaks is a second-order correction.
source: The max Lc has the higher weight in the probability estimation while the contribution of the correlation of the peaks (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1) is a second-order correction.
evidence: This describes the weighting in the Bayesian analysis.

claim: The same protein with different conformation is still properly classified by the Bayesian approach.
source: This means that the same protein with different conformation is still properly classified.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the robustness of the classification.

claim: Abundancy of the membrane proteins in the isolated membrane is a limiting factor.
source: Abundancy of the membrane proteins in the isolated membrane is also a limiting factor: the number of distinct membrane proteins that are present, for example, in hippocampal neurons is believed to be in the order of hundreds but with only few of them representing the majority of the expressed proteins.
evidence: This discusses a limitation related to protein abundance.

claim: With the approach, only 10 clusters were identified that are then assigned to some of the most abundant proteins in the respective contour length range.
source: With our approach indeed we identify only 10 clusters that are then assigned to some of the most abundant proteins in the respective contour length range (see Methods for a first-order assessment of the relation between the number of collected traces and the predicted dimension of a cluster).
evidence: This describes the outcome in terms of number of identified clusters.

claim: Functionalizing the cantilever tip could increase the yield of unfolding specific target proteins.
source: A way to mitigate this issue would be to functionalize the cantilever tip to increase the yield of unfolding specific target proteins.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future improvement.

claim: The specific functionalization strategy depends on the goal of the investigation.
source: The specific functionalization strategy really depends on the goal of the investigation.
evidence: This is a general statement about functionalization strategies.

claim: The goal of the present manuscript is to perform unbiased SMFS and the relatively low yield is an advantage.
source: The goal of the present manuscript is to perform unbiased SMFS and we think that the relatively low yield is an advantage in our case.
evidence: This explains the rationale for not functionalizing the tip.

claim: A high attachment rate would cause a higher probability of binding two proteins at the same time making the F-D curves analysis more complicated if not impossible to interpret.
source: A high attachment rate would cause a higher probability of binding two proteins at the same time making the F-D curves analysis more complicated if not impossible to interpret.
evidence: This is a reasoning about the consequences of high attachment rates.

claim: Attachment rates of 2% means that in first approximation double binding is also the 2% of the binding events so 0.04% overall, making the analysis less error-prone.
source: On the contrary, attachment rates of 2% means that in first approximation double binding is also the 2% of the binding events so the 0.04% overall: this makes the analysis less error-prone.
evidence: This is a calculation about the probability of double binding.

claim: An inherent characteristic of the isolation technique is that only the cytoplasmic side of the membrane is accessible.
source: Finally, an inherent characteristic of the isolation technique here presented is that only the cytoplasmic side of the membrane is accessible, and a method to reverse the membrane in order to perform the experiments from the extracellular side would be desired.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the membrane isolation technique.

claim: A method to reverse the membrane in order to perform the experiments from the extracellular side would be desired.
source: Finally, an inherent characteristic of the isolation technique here presented is that only the cytoplasmic side of the membrane is accessible, and a method to reverse the membrane in order to perform the experiments from the extracellular side would be desired.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future improvement.

claim: Despite the limitations, the study was able to classify tens of unfolding pathways, identify with high accuracy part of them, and reconcile some contrasting cryo-EM structures.
source: This work is a first step for the use of SMFS in native samples, but despite the limitations here reported, we were still able to classify tens of unfolding pathways, identify with high accuracy part of them, and we could also reconcile some contrasting cryo-EM structures.
evidence: This is a summary of the achievements despite limitations.

claim: The proposed methodology represents a genuine step in the direction of single-cell membrane proteomics.
source: We therefore believe that the proposed methodology represents a genuine step in the direction of single-cell membrane proteomics.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the significance of the work.
